elements.id-string-5: This paper addresses the challenge of industrial bin picking using entangled wire harnesses.
elements.id-string-6: Wire harnesses are essential in manufacturing but poses challenges in automation due to their complex geometries and propensity for entanglement.
elements.id-string-7: Our previous work tackled this issue by proposing a quasi-static pulling motion to separate the entangled wire harnesses.
elements.id-string-8: However, it still lacks sufficiency and generalization to various shapes and structures.
elements.id-string-9: In this paper, we deploy a dual-arm robot that can grasp, extract and disentangle wire harnesses from dense clutter using dynamic manipulation.
elements.id-string-10: The robot can swing to dynamically discard the entangled objects and regrasp to adjust the undesirable grasp pose.
elements.id-string-11: To improve the robustness and accuracy of the system, we leverage a closed-loop framework that uses haptic feedback to detect entanglement in real-time and flexibly adjust system parameters.
elements.id-string-12: Our bin picking system achieves an overall success rate of 91.2\% in the real-world experiments using two different types of long wire harnesses.
elements.id-string-13: It demonstrates the effectiveness of our system in handling various wire harnesses for industrial bin picking.

elements.id-string-16: Robotic bin picking has been developed for decades to automate the manufacturing process.
elements.id-string-17: It enables a robot to pick objects randomly placed in a bin and provide them to the assembly process.
elements.id-string-18: Utilizing bin picking in the assembly line can eliminate the need for preparing parts feeders and relieve human workers from tedious and repetitive workload.
elements.id-string-19: Existing bin picking approaches always focus on picking rigid objects \cite{kirkegaard2006bin,liu2012fast,buchholz2013efficient,domae2014fast,harada2016initial,matsumura2018learning,tachikake2020learning} while deformable objects pose new challenges.
elements.id-string-20: Wire harnesses are crucial components in the assembly of electric drive products.
elements.id-string-21: Due to their complex structures, which comprise both deformable cables and rigid components, wire harnesses in a cluttered environment are prone to entanglement.
elements.id-string-22: Developing bin picking system for entangled wire harnesses is extremely difficult.
elements.id-string-23: Object recognition and grasp detection becomes challenging in such complex scenarios involving with rich contact and environmental uncertainties.
elements.id-string-24: In the case of the robot grasping the end of the objects, executing disentangling motions becomes insufficient.
elements.id-string-25: Simulated training or obtaining models for wire harnesses still remains an open problem while training in the real world is time-consuming.
elements.id-string-26: Additionally, the manipulatable range of the robot in a standard bin picking cell has limited the maximum length of wire harnesses that can be handled.
elements.id-string-27: These difficulties led manufacturing industries to rely on human workers to manually separate entangled wire harnesses in the assembly processes.
elements.id-string-28: In our previous work \cite{zhang2022learning}, we learned a sequential policy that performs a circle-drawing trajectory to disentangle the wire harnesses.
elements.id-string-29: However, as the number of objects in a bin increases or when adapting to unseen objects types, the patterns of entanglement become unpredictable, making visual recognition and the circling motion insufficient.
elements.id-string-30: Moreover, wire harnesses often exceed the robot's reachable range, further diminishing the performance of quasi-static motion primitives for disentangling them.
elements.id-string-31: Therefore, more effective motion primitives and multiple sensing capabilities are highly demanded to ensure a robust, accurate and versatile bin picking system for wire harnesses.
elements.id-string-32: To further address these challenges, we present a bin picking system for entangled wire harnesses with the following key components:
elements.id-string-34: We propose two motion primitives: swing and regrasping, specifically designed for disentangling of long wire harnesses.
elements.id-string-35: The swing motion with a high velocity can dynamically extract the target from the clutter.
elements.id-string-36: On the other hand, regrasping enables the robot to grasp the target at its middle section, creating sufficient space for disentangling process.We present a closed-loop system that utilizes haptic feedback to detect entanglement in real-time and tunes the system parameters online.
elements.id-string-37: Unlike open-loop policies without error recovery, our system closes the loop by incorporating force feedback, enhancing the robustness and efficiency for picking entangled wire harnesses.

elements.id-string-102: We use a parametric action primitive to describe the movement of the robot.
elements.id-string-103: The action space for the swing primitive is $a=(\theta,\omega,n)$, where $\theta=(\theta_3,\theta_4,\theta_5)$ is the moving angles for the $i$-th joint in one robot arm.
elements.id-string-104: $\omega$ denotes the permissible angular velocity across all joints while $n$ indicates the number of times the swing motion is repeated.
elements.id-string-105: Specifically, $\theta_5$ denotes the angle for the yaw rotation for the last joint of the robot arm, which can be seen as a ``spinning'' motion.
elements.id-string-106: Meanwhile, $\theta_4,\theta_5$ are roll and pitch angles for the last arm joint and can perform a ``whipping'' motion.
elements.id-string-107: Three joints of the robot arm moves simultaneously and dynamically extract the objects from the clutter.
elements.id-string-108: Note that we initially set the values of $\theta$ and they can be tuned during the execution.
elements.id-string-109: The swing motion is illustrated in Fig. \ref{fig:motion}(a-b).
elements.id-string-111: Regrasp can switch the grasp pose to the middle of the target after the robot grasps the end of the object.

elements.id-string-114: Let the right arm of the robot, equipped with a force sensor, acts as the main arm while the left arm is the support arm.
elements.id-string-115: The main arm first grasps a wire harness and move to a pre-determine pose.
elements.id-string-116: Next, to determine the correct end of the object, the main arm's wrist spins by $\pi$ [rad] and we record the torque signals of both poses.
elements.id-string-117: The correct object end is determined by the minimal torque.
elements.id-string-118: Then, the support arm move to the pose where its gripper is below the main arm's gripper, moves downward and ensures the object is securely held in the gripper.
elements.id-string-119: It then closes the gripper and pulls the object upward.
elements.id-string-120: Finally, the main arm moves to the pose where its gripper is below the support arm's gripper and grasp the objects.
elements.id-string-121: After the support arm returns to its the initial pose, the regrasping attempt is completed and the main arm successfully adjusts the grasp pose.

elements.id-string-125: The workflow of our proposed system is shown in Fig. \ref{fig:overview} and Algorithm \ref{alg:system}.
elements.id-string-126: First, we obtain the depth image of the bin filled with wire harnesses and detect a set of collision-free grasp \cite{domae2014fast,zhang2022learning}.
elements.id-string-127: The robot then grasps the target and lifts it while monitoring the force $F_z$ in $z$ axis vertically to the workspace.
elements.id-string-128: If $F_z$ exceeds the threshold $F_\text{stop}$, the robot immediately stops and performs the swing motion to disentangle the target.
elements.id-string-129: Otherwise, If the haptic feedback does not provide an stopping point, meaning either the robot grasps a single wire harness or the regrasping motion is needed.
elements.id-string-130: Thus, to determine if the robot should execute the regrasping motion, we use $F_z=\{F_z^0,F_z^1,...,F_z^t\}$ over a time series $t$ recorded during the lifting process.
elements.id-string-131: We apply a median filter to $F_z$ and calculate the gradient $\dot{F}_z$.
elements.id-string-132: If $\dot{F}_z$ approximates zero, indicating that the target is too long to exert any forces on the gripper, the robot leverages regrasping to change the grasp position to the middle.
elements.id-string-133: Then, the robot tries to transport the wire harness to the goal bin while monitoring the force.
elements.id-string-134: However, if $F_z$ does not exceed $F_\text{stop}$ during transporting and also does not exceed $F_\text{fail}$ before dropping into the goal bin, the robot performs a successful attempt of picking a single wire harness.
elements.id-string-135: Otherwise, we increase the swing parameters $\theta$, adjust the force threshold $F_\text{stop},F_\text{fail}$ and restart from the beginning (lifting while monitoring $F_z$).
elements.id-string-136: Additionally, if the robot fails to disentangle the objects after two transporting attempts, it executes the regrasping motion.
elements.id-string-137: \SetKwInput{KwInput}{input}\SetKwInput{KwOutput}{output}\SetKwRepeat{Do}{do}{while}\SetKwFunction{FMain}{Update}\SetKwProg{Fn}{Function}{:}{}\Fn{\FMain{\rm $F_\text{stop},F_\text{fail},L$}}{\uIf{\rm not {stop when \texttt{lift} and \texttt{transport}}}{\tcp{Minimizes the gradient of $L$}$F_\text{fail} \gets \arg\min_{F} \dot{L}$ \;}\uIf{\rm not stop when \texttt{lift} \textbf{and} stop when \texttt{transport}}{$F_\text{stop} \leftarrow F_\text{stop} - \delta F$\;}}\caption{Online Parameter Tuning}
elements.id-string-139: In Line 15-17 of Algorithm \ref{alg:system}, we introduce an online parameter adjustment algorithm to improve the robustness of the robot.
elements.id-string-140: The initial force thresholds are manually set: $F_\text{stop}$ represents the minimal force where the entanglement occurs, while $F_\text{fail}$ approximates the weight of grasping a single object.
elements.id-string-141: Algorithm \ref{alg:param} outlines our online parameter tuning process.
elements.id-string-142: First, before the robot drops objects into the goal bin, we monitor the force $F_z^t$.
elements.id-string-143: If the robot successfully transports only one object without any stops during both lifting and transportation ($F_z^t<F_\text{fail}$), we adjust the value of $F_\text{fail}$.
elements.id-string-144: After each attempt in this scenario, we obtain a list $L$ of $F_z^t$.
elements.id-string-145: $F_\text{fail}$ is updated by minimizing the gradient of $L$ towards zero.
elements.id-string-146: The value of $F_\text{fail}$ gradually converges to a value and the updating process is stopped when the gradient no longer changes.
elements.id-string-147: Next, if the robot does not stop during lifting ($F_z^t<F_\text{fail}$) but encounters a stop during transporting ($F_z^t<F_\text{stop}$), it indicates that the threshold for detecting entanglement is not sensitive enough and should be tuned to a lower value.
elements.id-string-148: In this case, we set a residual force parameter $\delta F$ and adjust the threshold as follows: $F_\text{stop}=F_\text{stop}-\delta F$.
elements.id-string-149: In addition to the force thresholds, our algorithm also adjusts the swing parameters during each attempt.
elements.id-string-150: When the transporting process is unsuccessful, the robot will disentangle the grasped objects using increased swing angles.
elements.id-string-151: We increase the $\theta$ by a predefined residual angle $\delta \theta$, while ensuring that the adjustments remain within the velocity limits of the robot's arm.
elements.id-string-152: We also implement an additional motion \texttt{Swing}($(0,0,\hat{\theta_5}),\hat{\omega},2$) before the transporting process.
elements.id-string-153: This two-way spinning motion with pre-defined $\hat{\theta_5},\hat{\omega}$ can can provide additional assurance.

elements.id-string-172: We present two baselines and two ablated version of our method:
elements.id-string-173: \textbf{Lift-G}: This open-loop method uses Fast Graspability Evaluation (FGE) \cite{domae2014fast} to detect collision-free grasps and directly lifts the target after grasping, without incorporating haptic feedback.\textbf{Circle-A}: This open-loop method, described in \cite{zhang2022learning}, leverages ASPNet to infer the lowest action complexity of each grasp and execute a circling motion to disentangle the wire harnesses.\textbf{Ours-G}: Our closed-loop policy incorporates dynamic and bimanual manipulation with haptic feedback for real-time adjustments.
elements.id-string-174: It utilizes the FGE algorithm \cite{domae2014fast} for grasp detection.\textbf{Ours-A}: Our closed-loop policy optimizes the grasp pose using ASPNet \cite{zhang2022learning}.
elements.id-string-175: Instead of simply selecting the top rank from FGE, ASPNet evaluates the action complexity of each grasp and selects the lowest one.

elements.id-string-250: In this paper, we present a novel bin picking system specifically for grasping and separating entangled wire harnesses.
elements.id-string-251: Our closed-loop system utilizes dynamic manipulation with haptic feedback, enabling successful handling of complex entanglement scenarios.
elements.id-string-252: Through real-world experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our policy in disentangling various wire harnesses with high success rates.
elements.id-string-253: In future work, we will address failure cases by incorporating vision-guided regrasping motion or vision-haptic fusion policies.
elements.id-string-254: Additionally, we will enhance the perception module to obtain more precise and interpretable visual representations of the entangled deformable objects.
elements.id-string-255: Moreover, we will focus on optimizing the parameters of dynamic motion primitives to ensure both accuracy and safety in bin picking.
